newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: U.S. denies rift with Seoul over submarine crisis.
newsitem.headline: U.S. denies rift with Seoul over submarine crisis.

text.p: Washington's top Asia official on Saturday denied any rift with South Korea over how to respond to a North Korean submarine incursion, and he warned Pyongyang to "change its attitude" towards Seoul.
"There have been no rifts in our alliance," Winston Lord told a news conference at the end of a three-day visit to Seoul to display U.S. support for one of its closest Asian allies.

Reports suggesting the United States was at odds with South Korea were "highly exaggerated, misleading and can only tempt the North to try to drive a wedge between us", the U.S. Assistant Secretary of State said.
"This will never happen.
"U.S.-North Korean relations can only go so far without progress in Korean North-South relations," Lord said.
"We call upon North Korea to change course and change attitude. It's not too late to engage with the rest of the world."
Seoul's reaction to the intrusion of a North Korean submarine carrying 26 soldiers last month has been far more strident than the response from Washington.

South Korean politicians and the media have accused the United States of betraying its ally to preserve the gains of its policy of "constructive engagement" with Pyongyang, in particular a 1994 nuclear agreement.

Lord said the United States and South Korea had agreed to press ahead with implementation of the accord, under which North Korea agreed to scrap its suspected nuclear weapons programme in return for two light water nuclear reactors.
South Korean president Kim Young-sam had suggested Seoul was backing away from its commitments on the $5 billion nuclear deal that Seoul will largely finance.
Lord also said Washington and Seoul agreed to keep open the offer of four-party peace talks with North Korea, also including China.
"We do not wish to isolate North Korea. South Korea does not wish to isolate North Korea," he said.
"But of course in the current climate it cannot be business-as-usual," he said. There would be a "pause in the pace of our activities".

Although Lord described the situation on the Korean peninsula as serious and added that "it does carry some risks and dangers", his comments were far more measured than pronouncements by senior Seoul officials, including President Kim Young-sam, who has warned that the current crisis could result in "all-out war".
"I don't want to inflate the situation," Lord said.

He made no mention of any retaliation, although he said Washington and Seoul agreed to pursue action within the United Nations and noted the U.N. Security Council had unanimously agreed on a statement condemning Pyongyang.

South Korea has insisted Pyongyang must be made to pay for the incursion and on Friday said it would try to block international assistance to the North, where millions of people are going hungry following disastrous floods.
Lord again called on Pyongyang to release immediately U.S. citizen Evan Carl Hunziker, arrested as a spy for South Korea on charges that carry the death penalty.
"I call for his release immediately and that these ludicrous charges be dropped," he said.

Lord added that the United States was not prepared to link the case with the submarine incident. South Korea believes North Korea raised the spy issue to try to weaken Washington's resolve to back Seoul over the incursion.
